# How much fact-verification accuracy comes from seeing the contrast set?

## Abstract

Contrast sets test whether changing one fact changes a verifier’s answer. They also give a batch evaluator information unavailable when a claim arrives alone. We measured the value of that information while holding every model score fixed. On 712 FEVER Symmetric test examples, the original BART-large-MNLI checkpoint correctly classified 617 claim–evidence pairs when evaluated individually. An assignment constrained by the repeated claims reached 688. Constraining both repeated claims and repeated evidence reached 704. A RoBERTa-MNLI export also reached 704 from a higher individual baseline of 645. The joint decoder is invariant to any claim-only or evidence-only additive score. This identifies exactly which score variation can influence the batch decision. On 1,622 examples from real Wikipedia revisions in VitaminC, giving its authors’ ALBERT checkpoint paired context increased three-class accuracy from 85.02% to 88.59% (page-bootstrap difference 2.28–5.20 percentage points). These gains quantify access to the benchmark design. An evaluation intended to measure verification of an isolated claim should state whether test items are visible to one another.

## Question and related work

FEVER pairs English Wikipedia claims with verification labels. Schuster and colleagues demonstrated claim-only shortcuts and constructed symmetric claim–evidence examples to neutralize them. Gardner and colleagues proposed contrast sets and examined consistency across them. VitaminC uses near-identical evidence from revisions to test sensitivity to factual changes. These contributions motivate a different question. How much can the same verifier gain if its decisions, as well as its evaluation metric, depend on the other examples in a contrast set? We use standard constrained inference to quantify this advantage, give a characterization of the information the decoder removes, and compare isolated and batch decisions on identical IDs. [FEVER](https://aclanthology.org/N18-1074/) · [FEVER Symmetric](https://aclanthology.org/D19-1341/) · [Contrast sets](https://aclanthology.org/2020.findings-emnlp.117/) · [VitaminC](https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.52/) · [Integer linear programming inference](https://doi.org/10.1145/1102351.1102444)

ProToCo learns consistency across generated variants of a claim and evaluates real VitaminC revisions under few-shot and zero-shot supervision. He and colleagues construct larger FEVER and VitaminC claim sets and remove conflicting entries, evaluating the resulting sets against gold consistent subsets. Our unit of prediction is each released claim–evidence row. Every policy assigns a label to every row, and the fixed-score experiment varies which other released rows the decoder can see. These distinctions matter when attributing accuracy gains to additional context. Neither paper’s published aggregate is a head-to-head score on our held-out page cohort. [ProToCo](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.278/) · [Global consistency repair](https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-main.364/)

### What claim text can recover

A TF-IDF bigram logistic model on 145,446 FEVER training claims scored 52.47% accuracy and .5074 macro-F1 on the 19,998 shared-task development cases. Unigrams gave 50.34% and training-majority prediction gave 33.33%. Training strings also present in development after case and whitespace normalization were excluded. Of 795 SUPPORTS predictions made with confidence at least .90, 80.38% matched the release. This lexical replication reads no evidence. For any deterministic claim-only function, the best possible count on a fixed corpus is the sum of the largest label count at each distinct claim. On the binary FEVER Symmetric v0.2 test set, all 355 distinct claim strings have conflicting labels, and that bound is exactly 356/712. The three-class development benchmark and binary challenge have different populations and metrics. ## Fixed-score inference

Each FEVER Symmetric example is an edge between its exact claim string and exact evidence string. With the supplied evidence as premise, compute score $s_i$ as the entailment logit minus the contradiction logit. Let $x_i=1$ denote SUPPORTS. An independent decision takes $x_i=1$ when $s_i>0$. The claim-balanced decoder chooses the highest-scoring half of the examples attached to each claim. The joint decoder maximizes $\sum_i s_i x_i$ under a half-support constraint at every claim and evidence node. The solver sees strings and scores; it receives no gold label counts. All groups had even sizes, all solves reached optimality, and subsequent inspection confirmed that gold satisfies both constraints on both FEVER splits. Three-way decisions including neutral are reported separately.

**Why the joint decoder behaves differently.** Add any claim-specific offset $a_c$ and any evidence-specific offset $b_e$ to each edge score. Every feasible assignment then adds the identical objective constant $\sum_c a_c d_c/2 + \sum_e b_e d_e/2$, where $d$ is node degree. Its optimal assignments are unchanged. For an isolated two-by-two quartet, there are two feasible orientations. Only the contrast $s_{11}+s_{22}-s_{12}-s_{21}$ selects between them. All four labels can consequently be correct even when the individual decision boundary is poorly calibrated. The test release has 163 connected components, of which 150 are such quartets. If rows arrive independently with availability probability $q$, a given quartet row has access to all three partners with probability $q^3$. This is a design property, not an estimated traffic model.

We fit additive claim and evidence effects to the unlabeled edge scores by least squares. Removing them before joint decoding changed zero predictions for all three model implementations on both FEVER splits. Thresholding the resulting residuals at zero without any solver produced the same *count* correct as joint decoding in all six comparisons. That empirical equality of counts need not hold on other graphs. We resampled whole connected components so examples sharing an exact string stayed together. This interval describes variation among these observed components, including the rarer components larger than quartets. [Decoder](paired.py) · [Component analysis](components.py)

## FEVER Symmetric results

| Fixed model | Split | Rows | Correct, independent binary | Correct, claim-balanced | Correct, jointly balanced | Correct, unrestricted three-way |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| BART-large-MNLI, original | Dev | 708 | 622 | 686 | 704 | 547 |
| BART-large-MNLI, original | Test | 712 | 617 | 688 | 704 | 548 |
| RoBERTa-large-MNLI, quantized ONNX | Dev | 708 | 634 | 696 | 704 | 547 |
| RoBERTa-large-MNLI, quantized ONNX | Test | 712 | 645 | 694 | 704 | 572 |
| BART-large-MNLI, quantized ONNX | Dev | 708 | 482 | 590 | 640 | 11 |
| BART-large-MNLI, quantized ONNX | Test | 712 | 476 | 614 | 644 | 9 |

For original BART, the test gain was 12.22 percentage points (component-bootstrap 95% interval 9.29–15.12). For the RoBERTa export it was 8.29 points (5.76–10.88). They solved 149 and 148 of the 150 isolated test quartets completely. Restricting a model to the two available labels is already privileged task information. The independent binary column gives this benefit to every comparator before introducing group membership.

The initial experiment used two quantized ONNX exports. BART’s unusually low three-way score warranted checking the source checkpoint. Re-evaluation of the original weights yielded 548 correct three-way predictions on the same test set where the export yielded nine. Token IDs were verified equal example by example. The observed discrepancy involves the conversion, runtime and numeric representation together. These outputs cannot identify quantization alone as the cause. The published BART baseline in this paper is the original checkpoint. ## Transfer to VitaminC real revisions

We took the first 128 of 2,836 real-revision page titles sorted by SHA-256, preserving every example for each selected page. The resulting 1,622 rows have 811 SUPPORTS, 459 REFUTES and 352 NOT ENOUGH INFO labels. We ran the authors’ ALBERT-base-VitaminC-FEVER checkpoint with their 256-token limit and evidence–claim order. Independent predictions used the maximum of all three logits. For the 810 two-row groups with the same case ID and exact claim, a second policy forced one SUPPORTS prediction and gave the other row its highest-scoring alternative. Two remaining rows kept their independent decisions. No test labels enter this assignment.

| Policy | Correct SUPPORTS / 811 | Correct REFUTES / 459 | Correct NOT ENOUGH INFO / 352 | Total / 1,622 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Independent author checkpoint | 767 | 351 | 261 | 1,379 |
| Same logits, paired decision | 790 | 365 | 282 | 1,437 |

The net gain of 58 comprised 71 previously incorrect decisions repaired and 13 previously correct decisions lost. The expected one-support pattern failed in five groups. The paired rule therefore incurs an unavoidable accuracy cost on some legitimate examples. A 10,000-resample bootstrap by page gives a 95% interval of 2.28–5.20 points for the observed 3.58-point gain. These are real revisions selected and annotated for a contrastive dataset. The result transfers across two contrast-set constructions, with a task-trained comparator and a third label. It cannot establish the frequency of such pairs in incoming fact-checking traffic. ## Implications and reproducibility

A benchmark can both suppress claim-only shortcuts and supply a new source of information through its repeated examples. Publishing individual scores makes it possible to measure both regimes after evaluation. For a batch revision-review application, paired reasoning is a legitimate feature if the paired evidence really is available. For a verifier that receives one pair at a time, a jointly decoded benchmark score measures a different capability. These experiments use supplied evidence and English text. They measure neither retrieval quality nor historical verification in Vietnamese archives. None of the claims requires new human labels.

The initial claim-only results were known when planning the secondary comparisons. The full-precision check, component analysis and VitaminC transfer are identified separately. The data and original implementations remain attributable to their authors. [Secondary protocol and timing](paired_protocol.md) · [Reproduction commands](reproduce.md)

## Eight-checkpoint comparison on additional VitaminC pages

The 1,335 reserved examples span 128 real-revision pages. All 21 registered comparisons used the same test IDs and three-class endpoint. For the mixed-device replay we ran the three ALBERT-xlarge checkpoints in float32 on an RTX 4060 Ti, retaining the five CPU checkpoint outputs. The trained context stack with paired decoding scored 1,230 correct against 1,232 for a uniform average with the same decoder. The paired difference was −0.15 percentage points (page-bootstrap 95% interval −0.93 to +0.61). The candidate passed 12 of 21 registered comparisons. Using the literal development-page exclusion lowered the candidate to 1,223 correct, with the uniform rule still at 1,232. Both analyses failed the all-baseline criterion. Model choices and thresholds stayed frozen. The mixed-device run has its own artifact directory. [Protocol](confirmatory/protocol.md) · [Development-page correction](confirmatory/page_exclusion.md) · [Scores](confirmatory/device_replay/result.json) · [Corrected development set](confirmatory/device_replay/all_titles/result.json)

The completed original CPU run reproduced every predicted label in the mixed-device replay under both page-selection rules. All 22 methods agreed across devices on each of the 1,335 test IDs in each analysis. Independent scoring against the publisher labels reproduced all 21 paired intervals and adjusted decisions per analysis. These checks establish decision agreement for this cohort, including the candidate’s loss to the paired uniform ensemble.
